newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: S.Korean naphtha demand seen down over high price.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean naphtha demand seen down over high price.

text.p: South Korea's spot import demand for naphtha is set to slump because of high prices, with buyers looking to lock in term supplies instead, industry sources said on Wednesday.
Naphtha prices on Asia's benchmark open-specification forward contract have hovered at post-Gulf War highs since mid-November. On Tuesday, first-half February traded as high as $241.50 per tonne.
Second-half February, the most active trading period, was assessed on Tuesday at $239.00 per tonne.
Naphtha prices often track the progress of crude prices, but the relationship has failed in recent weeks as naphtha has plotted its own course.
"Crude has risen in a small range but naphtha prices have sky-rocketted artificially," complained a trader at South Korean petrochemical firm.
Traders said the differential, or crack, between Brent crude and Tokyo's open-spec market was usually between $50/$60 per tonne.
Earlier in December it ballooned to $76 and is currently assessed around $61.
But while naphtha prices are high, Korean petrochemical sources said they would seek to bring forward term contract purchases from domestic refiners.
This would reduce spot demand in February from the international market to four to five cargoes of up to 30,000 tonnes each, compared to up to 12 normally.
Sources said domestic supplies were ample as three South Korean refiners have shut down reformers, which use naphtha as a basic feedstock, due to weak profit margins.
Reformers are secondary refining units that convert naphtha into reformate, which in turn is used to make gasoline or is processed into petrochemical BTX.

Yukong Ltd, South Korea's largest refiner, indefinitely shut down a 15,000 barrel per day (bpd) reformer on Monday because of losses incurred from the high costs of the feedstock, a company source said.

A source from Hanwha Energy said a 30,000 bpd reformer was shut down due to "some minor technical problem" but had no definite start-up date. Hanwha has one other reformer, but with a small capacity of 5,000 bpd.
Although the sources said Ssangyong Oil's 45,000-bpd reformer was the first to shut down, a company source said Monday's shutdown, for less than a week, was scheduled.
South Korean traders said the shutdowns would mean that domestic refineries could have an extra two to four cargoes per month of naphtha supplies, starting as soon as December.
The start up of LG-Caltex Oil Corp's new 220,000-bpd crude-distillation unit at the end of December, would also boost domestic supplies, they said.
